findings.title: Unicode-equivalent destination names remain inside mirror deletion scope
findings.evidence: crates/blit-core/src/fs_enum.rs:205 — GlobBuilder::case_insensitive(true) uses globset's byte-regex mode, which folds ASCII, not Unicode. On case-insensitive macOS, mirror --exclude 'σ' with src/x/σ and dst/x/ς/saved.txt deleted saved.txt and exited 0. The filesystem identified both destination spellings as the same inode. The same failure reproduced for é versus É and NFC café versus NFD café. The ASCII cache/Cache control preserved saved.txt.
findings.predicted_failure: A mirror deletes pre-existing data inside an excluded destination subtree when its stored name differs by Unicode case or normalization. The shared destination deletion pass exposes local and daemon destinations to this failure.
findings.better_approach: Match destination name rules using the destination's supported case and normalization equivalence. Do not rely on globset's case-insensitive flag for Unicode folding. Add Unicode destination-survival tests.

findings.title: A glob component prevents protection of differently spelled destination descendants
findings.evidence: crates/blit-core/src/transfers/filter.rs:810 — respelled_below stops at the first glob component; crates/blit-core/src/fs_enum.rs:142 keeps path rules case-sensitive. Reproduced on macOS with src/x/cache and dst/x/Cache/saved.txt: both --exclude '**/cache' and the absolute --exclude '<src>/*/cache' omitted the source subtree but deleted saved.txt, exiting 0. The literal './x/cache' and bare 'cache' controls preserved it.
findings.predicted_failure: Valid relative and absolute glob exclusions still allow mirror to delete their excluded destination counterparts when stored spelling differs. This leaves cr-g3fix4-2 and the broader cr-g3fix-1 filesystem-case contract incomplete.
findings.better_approach: Preserve destination filesystem equivalence throughout path-rule matching, including components after globs, without expanding or rewriting wildcard syntax. Add survival coverage for '**/cache' and absolute wildcard paths.

findings.title: Rewriting an escaped separator changes recursive-glob semantics
findings.evidence: crates/blit-core/src/fs_enum.rs:300 and :326 — escaped '/' is emitted as a bare '/', turning '**\/cache' into '**/cache'. Globset parses the latter as a recursive prefix that also matches top-level cache; the original requires a preceding separator. A direct FileFilter comparison confirmed that cache/needed.txt changes from allowed to excluded. The built CLI's copy --exclude '**\/cache' omitted that file and exited 0.
findings.predicted_failure: Previously valid Unix exclusions acquire broader matching behavior, silently omitting additional files from copies or backups and incorrectly protecting additional paths from mirror deletion.
findings.better_approach: Translate escapes while preserving parsed glob semantics and rule anchoring, including the context-sensitive interpretation of '**'. Add equivalence tests for escaped separators adjacent to recursive wildcards.

findings.title: Bracket-aware pattern parsing is incorrectly applied to literal Windows roots
findings.evidence: crates/blit-core/src/transfers/filter.rs:390 and :415 — absolute_components applies the bracket-aware normalizer to the source root as well as the pattern. A parameterized Windows-rule probe on macOS used root 'C:\data[1\test]\src' and pattern 'C:/data[1/test]/src/cache'; relative_to_root returned None instead of ['cache']. The backslash between the root's two literal directory names was treated as a bracket-class member. through_resolved_root also stops at the bracket-bearing ancestor at line 335.
findings.predicted_failure: On Windows, an absolute exclude using forward slashes fails to relativize against an equivalent backslash-spelled source root whose directory components contain brackets spanning a separator. The command reports the exclude as unmatchable and proceeds without excluding the requested subtree.
findings.better_approach: Tokenize filesystem roots and resolved prefixes as literal paths, normalizing every native separator. Reserve bracket-aware tokenization for user pattern text, and test mixed separators with bracket-bearing root components.
